title: Workplace Gossip: When It Helps and When It Hurts
paragraphs: Workplace gossip has a bad reputation — and for good reason!
Stephanie Joseph learned that firsthand when someone at work started a false rumor that she and a married colleague were romantically involved.
"I'm thinking to myself, this is crazy," said Joseph, who was then 20 and barely knew the man.
Gossip can damage the reputation of both the person being discussed and the person spreading it. But workplace experts say it can also have benefits.
In some cases, gossip can warn coworkers about problematic behavior, and can even help build workplace relationships.
Rebecca Greenbaum, a professor at Rutgers University who studies workplace gossip, said people often share information to connect with others who understand their experiences.
And gossip doesn't have to mean sharing bad news or negative views. Coworkers may praise someone behind their back, or share useful information about the workplace.
For example, sharing that a coworker is in a bad mood may let colleagues know to give that person some space or be especially nice, Greenbaum said.
But too much gossip can come at a cost.
Etiquette expert Mariah Humbert said someone who often talks negatively about others may lose coworkers' trust.
Gossip can also take up valuable work time and reduce productivity. Often, venting to someone outside the workplace may be a better option, experts say.

So how can you avoid getting involved in gossip? Well, you can try using a simple phrase such as "I hear you" or "I don't know all the details" before moving the conversation to other topics, such as weekend plans, restaurants, travel or sports.
And while some gossip at work may be unavoidable, people should think about whether what they're repeating is true, and whether they'd say it directly to the person involved.
"Workplace gossip is going to happen, but let's try to keep it as harmless as possible because it could be you," Joseph said. "It could be any of us at any time."
